extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television fans, and researchers interested in satirical/clip-show television formats
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive guidelines and implicit production standards for a satirical television clip-show (like The Soup), covering show format, segment structure, recurring characters/gags, clip editing practices, original skits, and broadcast constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show format and segment flow
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show features the host on a green-screened set with a screen to their right. The show is broken up into various segments that focus on themes such as reality television shows or shows on E!. The host introduces each clip, which is then played, then comments on the clip before moving on to the next one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core structural rule: each segment centers on a theme, follows the introduce–play–comment pattern, and uses the green-screen set to juxtapose host and clips. The 2020 revival adds a second camera/stage-right auxiliary display for alternate presentation. This flow shapes pacing and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live audience involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a live audience on the show, composed of a small group of E! employees, their family, and friends, along with the typical production personnel. The audience is involved in the show, laughing and cheering along with the clips."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a present audience (even if small or production-staff-based) to supply audible reactions and to create a live-comedy rhythm; audience responses are integral to timing and emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripted but improvisational tone
rubrics_metrics.description: "Although the show is scripted, a large portion of it is ad-libbed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance prepared material (written bits/segues) with improvisation around clips. Encourage host spontaneity and reactive quips to preserve freshness and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recurring characters and in-house cast
rubrics_metrics.description: "During its original 2004–2015 run, The Soup used its own cast of recurring characters. They include Mankini..., a dancing maxi pad (Tess Rafferty...), two nerds who dress as Star Wars characters, an intern named Matt..., Jewbacca..., and 'Spaghetti Cat'... Executive producer Edward Boyd's chihuahua Lou appeared regularly in segment openings..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a small stable of recurring characters/bit-players to appear across episodes for continuity, running gags, and quick visual jokes; integrate them into openings, transitions, and bespoke skits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core regular segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular segments include: "Chat Stew" (clips from talk shows), "Chicks, Man" (female celebrity news), "Reality Show Clip Time!" (clips from reality shows), "Let's Take Some E!" (clips from other E! programs), and the show-ending "Clip of the Week" (the best clip shown on TV in the past week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a small set of reliable recurring segments that map to topical niches (talk shows, reality, network-specific content). Reserve a culminating segment (e.g., Clip of the Week) to close with a standout moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized and recurring topical segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Other recurring segments include: "What's Pissing Off Steve Edwards This Week?", "Tales from Home Shopping", "Oprah's Vajayjay", "What the Kids Are Watching" (and spinoffs "What the Old Folks Are Watching" / "What Your Boyfriend's Looking At"), "Clippos Magnificos" (telenovelas), "Souper Fantastic Ultra Wish Time!" (Japanese programs), "Cyber Smack" (viral internet videos), "My Stories" (soap opera clips), and many more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized segments to mine particular sources or subcultures for repeatable jokes; segments can spawn spin-offs or content verticals (e.g., Web Soup). Tailor titles/intros to signal comedic framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring jokes and comedic targets
rubrics_metrics.description: The show has a number of recurring jokes and segments. One of the most frequent jokes is Joel McHale making fun of Ryan Seacrest. Joel also spoofed actors like David Caruso, joked about Tyra Banks, mocked Spencer Pratt's appearance, joked about the ages of Larry King and Regis Philbin, and regularly berated or "abused" interns as a running gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish repeatable targets (celebrities, TV tropes) and consistent punchlines or shticks so audiences come to expect certain callbacks; exercise awareness of taste and potential offense when repeating personal-targeted humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clip selection and reuse (stock reaction clips)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of clips have been repeatedly shown on The Soup (examples: Oprah saying "My va-jay-jay is painin'!", Whitney Houston yelling "Kiss My Ass!", Ann Curry's repetitive greeting, Kendra Wilkinson laughing). Shorter clips are sometimes used as interjections; reaction clips (e.g., Ryan Seacrest "Hell no, say what") are used as recurring punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate a library of recognizable reaction clips and favorites that can be reused as running gag elements and beat-fillers; short clips function as rhythmic punctuation and audience in-jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edited clips and transparent 'doctoring' for comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Soup will often make blatant and obvious edits to clips of shows, often killing off characters... McHale will often punctuate the clip by saying 'We doctored that.' However, if a clip was shown that may have made the audience think that it was edited by The Soup for broadcast while watching it, McHale would state before hand 'We did not doctor this.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ obvious edits/splices to create new comedic contexts, but use on-air disclaimers to avoid misleading viewers about what is authentic. Make the edits part of the joke (self-aware), and be explicit when edits might be construed as deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original skits, spoofs, and fake trailers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Original skits are integrated into the show as responses or jokes to clips. Fake movie trailers and advertisements are created as spoofs to segments or clips. Among the movies spoofed are Spider-Man 3..., Harry Potter..., Made of Honor..., Righteous Kill..., Mamma Mia..., Beverly Hills Chihuahua..., Quarantine..., Prom Night..., Fast & Furious..., and a Tyler Perry movie."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Augment clip commentary with produced original content (sketches and spoof trailers) to broaden comedic range and to create shareable bits; tie spoofs directly to clips/themes being lampooned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of audio/sound-bite devices and props for punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The program uses recurring sound clips and props as punchlines — examples include a gun sound effect when "shooting" an intern, the "That's Right It's Steven Seagal" sound clip followed by Joel drinking a floating energy drink, and musical bits (e.g., Jeffrey Osborne's "On the Wings of Love" to mock The Bachelor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate signature audio cues and simple props to punctuate jokes and create recognizable running bits; ensure timing with audience reaction and clip editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast and runtime constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: "Running time: 22 minutes. Camera setup: Single-camera. Network: E!. Production company: Mission Control Media. Original release..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design episode structure to fit a ~22-minute half-hour broadcast slot (including act breaks for ads if applicable); single-camera setup and network expectations affect pacing, segment length, and production values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format adaptability and spin-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: The format has produced spin-offs and tailored versions (The Dish, Sports Soup, Web Soup, Celebrity Soup, The Soup Investigates) and region-specific broadcasts (e.g., Celebrity Soup in the UK).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clip-show/satire format is adaptable: customize segment focus, host voice, and running gags to suit different subject-matter verticals, networks, or international audiences while retaining core introduce–clip–comment mechanics.
